Catch You Later
KACH yoo LAY-ter
phrase (Boomer slang)
Catch in the sense of meeting up with someone ("I’ll catch you at lunch") + later. Catch you later — goodbye for now — is twentieth-century American colloquial, very common from the 1960s–70s, along with its clipped forms later, laters, and catch ya, and its CB-era cousin catch you on the flip side.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Catch you later is a casual goodbye that assumes a next time: "See you around; we’ll pick this up again." The Christian observation: every goodbye rests on an assumption Scripture asks us to say out loud. We assume there will be a later. James gently corrects the habit of talking as if tomorrow were ours: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city ... Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:13–15). "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Pro 27:1). The older generation’s farewell, "Lord willing," said exactly that. But Scripture also gives believers a later that is certain. At the graveside Paul comforts the church: "we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1Th 4:17–18). For Christians, every goodbye — even the last one — is truly "catch you later." A grandmother who says it at the end of a phone call, and a grandson who says it at her bedside in the hospital, can both mean it with the full weight of the resurrection.

Webster 1828 Definition

Mid-20th-c. American goodbye (common 1960s–70s; also later, catch you on the flip side) that assumes a next time — an assumption Scripture qualifies with "If the Lord will" (Jas 4:15) and fulfils for believers in the reunion of 1Th 4:17.

CATCH YOU LATER, phr. (American colloquial, 20th c.; common Boomer use 1960s–70s) Goodbye; see you again. Also later, laters, catch ya; compare catch you on the flip side.

Webster (1828) — LATE, adverb 1. After the usual time, or the time appointed; after delay; as, he arrived late 2. After the proper or usual season. This year the fruits ripen late

Decode for families: add the old words, "Lord willing," and the phrase becomes a confession of faith.

Key Scripture

Jas 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Jas 4:15 — "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that."

Pro 27:1 — "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth."

1Th 4:17 — "Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord."

1Th 4:18 — "Wherefore comfort one another with these words."

Modern Corruption

A friendly goodbye that quietly presumes on tomorrow; Scripture teaches the believer to say "If the Lord will" and gives him a certain later in the resurrection.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong with catch you later. Its only weakness is the one James names: it speaks of tomorrow as if we owned it. Earlier generations of Christians wrote "D.V." — Deo volente, God willing — on their letters and plans. That habit was not superstition; it was humility, and it is worth reviving in our own speech.

The deeper comfort is that the Christian’s goodbyes are never final. Paul wrote 1Th 4:17–18 to grieving believers who wondered whether their dead were lost, and his answer was a reunion — "together with them" — in the presence of the Lord. Every Christian funeral is, in the end, a "catch you later."

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old North French cachier (to chase, to capture) → catch (to meet up with) + Old English læt (late) → 20th-c. American catch you later.

expand to see more

Old North French cachier — to chase, to hunt; English catch — to seize; to meet up with

Old English læt — slow, late (see Late)

20th-c. American colloquial: catch you later; clipped later

1970s: catch you on the flip side (CB and radio slang)

Latin Deo volente — "God willing" (compare Jas 4:15)

""Grandma always ends a call with ‘Catch you later, Lord willing.’ We used to laugh. Now we say it too.""

"Ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that (Jas 4:15)."
